title: What Does Your Phone Actually Send When You Send an Emoji?
sources: Unicode Consortium FAQ 'Emoji and Pictographs' (unicode.org/faq/emoji_dingbats.html) and Wikipedia 'Emoji': each emoji is a Unicode character (a code point); the Unicode Consortium encodes them and each vendor draws its own image in its emoji font
Unicode chart U1F600 / codepoints.net U+1F602: FACE WITH TEARS OF JOY = U+1F602

emoji.codes 'Why emojis look different on different platforms' and emojifyi 'How emoji rendering works across platforms': the same code point is rendered with Apple Color Emoji, Noto Color Emoji etc.; if a device's font lacks the character it shows an empty box ('tofu') or a question mark
Unicode Technical Standard #51 (Unicode Emoji) and emojifyi 'What are ZWJ sequences?': family emoji are ZWJ sequences, several person emoji joined by the invisible zero width joiner U+200D

lines.text: When you send an emoji, does your phone actually send a tiny picture?
lines.caps: WHEN YOU *SEND | AN *EMOJI | DOES YOUR *PHONE | ACTUALLY *SEND | A TINY *PICTURE?

lines.text: Every emoji has its own code in a giant list called Unicode,
lines.caps: *EVERY EMOJI | HAS ITS OWN *CODE | IN A *GIANT LIST | CALLED *UNICODE

lines.text: so the laughing crying face is really code one F six oh two.
lines.caps: SO THE *LAUGHING | CRYING *FACE | IS REALLY *CODE | ONE *F602

lines.text: Your friend's phone reads that code
and draws the emoji with its own artwork,
which is why the same emoji looks different on iPhone and Android.
lines.caps: WHICH IS *WHY | THE *SAME EMOJI | LOOKS *DIFFERENT | ON *IPHONE | AND *ANDROID

lines.text: And if their phone is too old to know that code,
lines.caps: AND IF *THEIR | PHONE IS TOO *OLD | TO *KNOW | THAT *CODE

lines.text: they just see an empty box.
the family emoji is really several people,
glued together with an invisible character.
So that heart you just sent? It was just a number.
lines.caps: SO THAT *HEART | YOU JUST *SENT? | IT WAS *JUST | A *NUMBER
